item.title: Iraq Under Pressure After Drone Strikes Close Key Saudi Pipeline
item.description: Iraq is moving to contain the fallout from attacks that caused the closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, after the strikes were found to have been launched from inside the country.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Iraq is moving to contain the fallout from attacks that caused the closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, after the strikes were found to have been launched from inside the country.Early on Saturday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi fired the operations commander of Maysan province and ordered an investigation after determining that attacks targeting the pipeline came from a site within the region, which borders Iran, according to a statement.Saudi Arabia shut the conduit as a precautionary measure on Friday after several drones attacked the major pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions, according to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs.Iraq has been under pressure to try and rein in local Iran-backed militias from helping other proxy groups across the region, but has had little success and its territory has become a key base for Tehran’s retaliation across the Gulf.The East-West pipeline has become a crucial lifeline for Saudi Arabia’s oil exports, particularly since disruption from the Iran war. The 7 million barrel-a-day conduit quickly reached full capacity earlier this year after tanker traffic came to a near standstill in the Strait of Hormuz.Iran-backed Houthi forces have upped the pressure though, progressing along Yemen’s Red Sea coast toward the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, gaining ground while continuing missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, forcing it to halt several energy sites. If the group increases its control over the area, they’d have more power to disrupt shipping through another energy chokepoint, adding pressure to already increased oil prices. It would also threaten Saudi Arabia’s own efforts to protect its economy from regional conflict.Oil prices were little changed after the Saudi ministry statement, with Brent futures trading at about $105 a barrel. Brent surged on Thursday, almost reaching $110, on speculation about the impact of the latest conflict on energy supplies in the region.Since the drone attacks, Iraq has also ordered the closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iran as a precautionary measure, Reuters reported, citing unidentified security sources. More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: DR Congo's World Cup exploits encourage more players to join their cause
item.description: Democratic Republic of Congo's success at this year’s World Cup has seen a bevy of European-born players added to their squad as coach Sebastien Desabre seeks to expand the player pool and build on their last-32 place at the finals in North America.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gleeson
item.content:encoded:
Democratic Republic of Congo's success at this year’s World Cup has seen a bevy of European-born players added to their squad as coach Sebastien Desabre seeks to expand the player pool and build on their last-32 place at the finals in North America. DR Congo will later this month play their first matches since the World Cup, where they were 15 minutes away from an [USN:L8N4331WK TEXT:"upset win over England in Atlanta"], when they begin the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers. Six new players from European clubs have since been added to the squad to face Equatorial Guinea in Kinshasa on September 24 and Zimbabwe away in Harare four days later. Former Manchester United centre back Willy Kambwala, now at Italian club Como, was named along with Ezechiel Banzuzi (Leipzig), Stanis Idumbo (AS Monaco), Jordy Makengo (Freiburg), Noah Mbamba (Lorient) and Kevin Pedro (Saint-Etienne). Banzuzi (Netherlands), Idumbo and Mbamba (Belgium) plus Pedro (France) have all been capped at junior level and would need FIFA's permission to switch international eligibility. None of the four have yet been approved, according to FIFA’s Change of Association Platform. DR Congo have in the past named players in the squad without securing their agreement, or a formal switch of allegiances. However, Desabre has been on a charm offensive across Europe in recent months, seeking to persuade players of Congolese heritage to commit to an international future with the Leopards. DR Congo went past the group phase at the World Cup for the first time at this year's tournament in Canada, Mexico and the United States. Banzuzi used social media this week to announce his switch to the DR Congo team after playing at under-21 level for the Netherlands, where he was born. He posed for a picture with a Congolese shirt.

View this post on Instagram

DR CONGO LOOKING TO BUILD FORMIDABLE SQUAD Desabre plans to use friendlies against Uganda on October 2 and October 5 to try and persuade even more players to join, seeking to build a formidable squad with less than a year to the Cup of Nations finals in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda next June. For the two clashes against Uganda, six more new players from European clubs have been invited, including Ajax Amsterdam teenager Jorthy Mokio, capped by Belgium last year, and two England under-20 internationals, Paris Maghoma and Stephy Mavididi, who play in the Championship (second tier). Former Dutch under-21 international Anthony Musaba, who is at Championship side Norwich City, is also on the list. Mokio earlier this year expressed his desire to play for the Congolese but because he featured in the Nations League for Belgium in March 2025, he must wait three years. Players under 21 years old, with no more than three competitive caps at senior level, can switch allegiance, but there is a three-year cooling-off period. The two matches against Uganda are not competitive, leaving a grey area for Mokio to begin integrating into the team, even if his official debut can only happen in 18 months' time.

item.title: Red Sox turn to Ranger Suarez in bid to regroup vs. Royals
item.description: The Boston Red Sox hope to shake a recent skid when they continue a three-game weekend series against the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Boston Red Sox hope to shake a recent skid when they continue a three-game weekend series against the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon. Boston (80-68) left eight men on base and went 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position en route to a 3-2 loss on Friday. The setback was the club's third in a row and fifth in the last six home games since Sept. 1. "We need to do more, particularly in the early part of games," said Boston interim manager Chad Tracy, whose team is still five games clear in a wild-card position. Mickey Gasper homered while Trevor Story and Wilyer Abreu each had a double, but Boston managed just one hit after the fifth inning allowed the Royals (66-82) to clinch their third win in five games following a 1-5 stretch. Tracy looks to left-hander Ranger Suarez (6-4, 3.44 ERA) to build upon his third scoreless start of at least seven innings this season. After allowing 18 earned runs in his previous six starts, Suarez scattered five hits, walked one and struck out three to lead the Red Sox to a 1-0 win at the Baltimore Orioles last Friday. "Literally, I've been waiting for (that type of) start for a while," Suarez said. "The (previous) three or four...I (wasn't) able to complete six. So, to be able to have a start like that and have a strong end of the year, that's what I'm looking for." A first-inning solo home run by Gasper was all that the left-hander needed for support in his last outing. The New Hampshire native repeated the feat on Friday for his ninth homer in the last 21 games. Suarez has enjoyed success in two career starts against the Royals, going 1-0 with a 1.93 ERA and nine strikeouts over 9 1/3 innings. Earlier this season, he allowed one run in 4 1/3 innings of l in a no-decision on May 19. Kansas City rode early offense off American League Cy Young candidate Sonny Gray to the series-opening triumph, which was its seventh in the last 10 road games. Carter Jensen and Salvador Perez each had an RBI as part of their two-hit performances, with Jensen scoring a run after each of his first two at-bats. Jensen's two doubles give him 56 extra-base hits on the season, the most among AL rookies. "(The win) felt great," Jensen said. "Get off to a hot start for sure. Good start to the road trip and getting a win. Yeah, it was a fun game all around." In manager Matt Quatraro's eyes, it was an earned victory. "I mean, that was a grinder," he said. Right-hander Randy Dobnak (3-3, 2.54) is slated to make Saturday's start for the Royals. The 31-year-old has allowed two or fewer earned runs in eight of his 10 starts since joining the rotation in mid-July. He earned his first win in over a month on Sunday against the Toronto Blue Jays, allowing just one run in his third straight six-inning outing. "He sinks it. He slides it. He sweeps it. He does all of it," first baseman Vinnie Pasquantino said of Dobnak, who the Royals acquired in a June 17 trade from the Seattle Mariners and promoted from Triple-A Omaha on July 1. "He's been a great addition. He's great in the clubhouse." Dobnak is 0-1 with a 2.25 ERA in two career appearances (four innings) against the Red Sox, with his lone start coming as an opener with the Minnesota Twins in 2019. --Field Level Media

item.title: Blue Jays bid to put 'best foot forward' in rematch vs. Orioles
item.description: The visiting Baltimore Orioles have a chance to draw even with the Toronto Blue Jays on Saturday afternoon in the crowded race for the final wild-card spot in the American League.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The visiting Baltimore Orioles have a chance to draw even with the Toronto Blue Jays on Saturday afternoon in the crowded race for the final wild-card spot in the American League. The Orioles (72-76) recorded a 7-4 victory over the Blue Jays (73-75) in the opener of a three-game series on Friday night to pull to 4-4 in the season series. The teams will play again in Toronto on Saturday afternoon. "Everything is high stakes," Blue Jays manager John Schneider said. "It's not going to be easy, but I think how you handle it is you continue to find ways to put your best foot forward and put guys in position to succeed. That's it, really." In the wild-card race, the Blue Jays fell two games behind the Cleveland Guardians, who posted a 5-2 victory over the Minnesota Twins on Friday. "September baseball, it's the best," said Heston Kjerstad, who contributed an RBI single in Baltimore's five-run second inning on Friday. "We're playing for something that's really important. We all want to clinch a playoff spot. We're all playing hard. We're all doing everything we can to make that happen." Baltimore's Dylan Beavers led off Friday's game with a home run against Max Scherzer and added a two-run single in the second. Coby Mayo added a seventh-inning homer. Orioles starter Chris Bassitt, who helped the Blue Jays reach the World Series last season, allowed two runs in five-plus innings on Friday. "Is every game a must-win? No," Bassitt said. "But you kind of have to treat every game right now like a must-win. We don't have a lot of games left. We have a little bit more to go from a wild-card standpoint. So yeah, just playing clean, but playing with the sense of urgency that we need to, being smart, yeah, every game is really important." Right-hander Kyle Bradish (7-13, 3.91 ERA) will start for the Orioles on Saturday. He is 2-4 with a 4.94 ERA in 10 career appearances (all starts) vs. the Blue Jays and is 1-1 with a 4.09 ERA in two starts against them this season. The Blue Jays will turn to right-hander Spencer Miles (6-2, 2.77) to start Saturday's game. He struck out three batters and did not allow a hit over two scoreless innings on Tuesday in his team's 4-2 victory over the A's. Miles is 1-1 with a 9.82 ERA in two appearances (one start) vs. the Orioles this season, his first in the majors. The Blue Jays are expected to use right-hander Spencer Arrighetti (7-9, 5.12 ERA) after Miles. Arrighetti is 1-1 with a 1.62 ERA in three career starts against the Orioles. Rookie Brett Bateman provided some of the few Blue Jays highlights in the series opener. He had three hits, including his first major league home run, a two-run shot with two outs in the ninth inning. Toronto's Vladimir Guerrero Jr. continued his struggles, going 1-for-4 with an infield hit and a walk. He helped squelch a potential rally in the first inning when catcher Samuel Basallo picked him off first base. Alejandro Kirk followed with a walk that would have loaded the bases. "(First-base coach) Mark Budzinski was on it, kind of yelling. He didn't hear him," Schneider said of Guerrero. "He just got out too far. Baserunning plays like that can shift momentum a little bit. It could have been a little bit different after Kirk walks. He got out too far, and they made a play." The Blue Jays made a change in their outfield on Friday. Jesus Sanchez, who had been a defensive liability, was designated for assignment, while Rudy Martin Jr. was promoted from Triple-A Buffalo and was used as a pinch runner in the ninth. --Field Level Media

item.title: Hamilton and Bearman crash in final Spanish GP practice, Antonelli top
item.description: Title contender Lewis Hamilton crashed his Ferrari in final practice for the Spanish Grand Prix at Madrid's new Formula One circuit on Saturday, halting the session with just over half an hour left, while Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli was fastest.
item.dc:creator: Alan Baldwin
item.content:encoded: Title contender Lewis Hamilton crashed his Ferrari in final practice for the Spanish Grand Prix at Madrid's new Formula One circuit on Saturday, halting the session with just over half an hour left, while Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli was fastest. The seven-times world champion, a distant third in the overall standings, locked up and went into the barriers at the final corner. Hamilton managed to reverse out and tried to get the damaged Ferrari back to the Madring pitlane, virtually a whole lap, while ignoring team instructions to stop. The Briton eventually did pull over, with the front wing still wedged under the car which also had a punctured front right tyre. "Stop the car. Stop in the safest place possible," he had been told earlier. "If I can make it back I will. If not, I will do it safely," replied Hamilton, who returned to the pits on the back of a moped after parking up. The session was red-flagged and the clock then temporarily stopped for barrier repairs with 15 minutes to go. When it re-started, Antonelli knocked Ferrari's Charles Leclerc off the top of the timesheets with a time of one minute and 32.797 seconds, 0.166 quicker than the Monegasque. Antonelli is 66 points clear of teammate and closest rival George Russell after 13 rounds. Haas's Bearman then brought out the red flags again in the final minute when he spun and hit the barriers backwards at Turn 11, the approach to La Monumental, the circuit's banked signature curve. McLaren's Oscar Piastri was third quickest ahead of reigning champion and teammate Lando Norris with Red Bull's Max Verstappen fifth and Russell sixth. Red Bull's Liam Lawson and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg were seventh and eighth, with Hamilton ninth and Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto completing the top 10. Qualifying followed two hours later and will be crucial for Sunday's race, with overtaking likely to be difficult on a challenging layout that Russell said on Friday had less margin for error than Monaco because of the close walls but higher speeds involved. "Nobody really knows what to expect. The session was tight. It’s about putting a lap together without mistakes and traffic," said Mercedes boss Toto Wolff.

item.title: UK PM's office says position on Irish unity unchanged after Trump comments
item.description: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's position on Irish unification remains unchanged, a spokesperson for his office said on Saturday, following comments by U.S. President Donald Trump that he would "love" to see a united Ireland.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's position on Irish unification remains unchanged, a spokesperson for his office said on Saturday, following [USN:S8N42A05F TEXT:"comments"] by U.S. President Donald Trump that he would "love" to see a united Ireland. Responding to questions from lawmakers in parliament on Wednesday about a possible border poll in Northern Ireland, Burnham said: "I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one." A spokesperson for Burnham's office said on Saturday the prime minister's remarks still stood after Trump told reporters after [USN:L6N454021 TEXT:"a meeting"] with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin that unification would happen eventually.

item.title: Hidden crypto farm in Mexican mountains puts spotlight on cartel funding
item.description: Crypto mining—which uses powerful computers to generate virtual assets such as Bitcoin—has become a new tool for organized criminal groups and a new front in Mexico’s fight against them.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Morland, Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: Nestled in the lush green mountains of Central Mexico, next to a sparsely traveled gravel road, few people had reason to wander close enough to hear the loud, mechanical whirring of a clandestine cryptocurrency farm. What led police to the ramshackle building, suspected of mining virtual coins to launder illicit funds, was not only the noise but the vast amount of electricity needed to power and cool hundreds of specialized computing units, at levels far surpassing the needs of the small communities scattered around the Sierra Norte region of Puebla state. Crypto mining — which uses powerful computers to generate virtual assets such as bitcoin — represents a new frontier in Mexico's fight against organized criminal groups, which have [USN:L1N2IO25U TEXT:"extended their reach"] beyond drug trafficking and extortion into the murkier realm of financial crime. In Puebla, authorities discovered 300 graphics processing units (GPUs), 80 medium-voltage terminals and eight satellite antennae — all geared to compete against millions of other machines to solve puzzles and create valuable new crypto coins. While a relatively modest operation by international commercial standards, it is the fourth such crypto farm uncovered in the area since early last year. "Drug cartels appear to have reached a new level of sophistication," said David Saucedo, a Mexico-based security analyst, adding that setting up such an operation would have required technical expertise and backing from a well-financed group, such as one of Mexico's most powerful cartels. Mexico's federal attorney's office declined to comment, citing an active investigation. ELECTRICITY THEFT FUELS OPERATIONS Globally, illicit cryptocurrency transactions more than doubled in 2025, with addresses linked to criminal activity receiving an estimated $154 billion, up from $59 billion a year earlier, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, which analyzed transaction volumes sent to illicit wallet addresses. Chainalysis attributed much of the increase to a surge in transactions linked to sanctions evasion, including payments involving sanctioned governments. As more people and institutions worldwide adopt virtual currency, most within the confines of the law, Latin American cartels are among those increasingly using crypto transfers and mining operations to launder money, said Caio Motta, the firm's Latin American specialist. "These locations will have very cheap electricity, or be in an area under the influence of organized crime so they're able to steal electricity and establish a large infrastructure to mine cryptocurrency," Motta said. Electricity is the biggest cost for mining crypto, as energy prices have increased and the process of minting a single unit of virtual currency has become more resource-intensive. The University of Cambridge's Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index estimates the cost of minting one bitcoin — the most widely used cryptocurrency — at nearly $45,000. This would still bring a substantial profit when sold at current prices of around $78,000. "If they were stealing the electricity, the main costs of the operation would be, well — nothing," said Samuel Leon, an expert in energy theft at Mexico's Iberoamericana University, referring to the Puebla operation. Mexican authorities said they are investigating whether the crypto farm was stealing electricity from a nearby hydroelectric dam. HIDDEN IN REMOTE MOUNTAIN TERRAIN The bushy forests and scattered communities of the Sierra Norte, where the Puebla crypto farm was found, made for an ideal hiding spot. Two people living in neighboring communities, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, told Reuters that the whirring noise could be heard one kilometer (0.6 mile) away. The crypto farm was located approximately twice that distance from the nearest village. Three other similar crypto farms were found last year in the vicinity of the nearby hydroelectric dam in northern Puebla. Local authorities said they are collaborating with nearby states to investigate the possibility of more hidden operations. Similar raids have taken place in Brazil, the U.S. and Southeast Asia, including a major bitcoin mining operation in Thailand that spanned five provinces. According to Motta of Chainalysis, rising global cryptocurrency use will likely push crypto-related crime to new records in the years ahead, as virtual currencies become more accessible even as investigators improve their ability to trace online transactions. "Law enforcement agencies are becoming far more equipped to fight organized crime using cryptocurrency," he said.

item.title: China's Xi urges BRICS to take on peacemaking role in Middle East war
item.description: He said China will assume the group's chairmanship next year.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Chinese President Xi Jinping urged the BRICS bloc to be a peacemaker in the Middle East conflict , in an address to [USN:L6N45402F TEXT:"a summit"] of member countries in New Delhi on Saturday. China will work with other BRICS members in that role, as the war "does not serve the common interests of the international community", state-run CCTV quoted Xi as saying. BRICS groups Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates. It was [USN:L6N4510UT TEXT:"set up"] in 2009 to challenge a world order dominated by the United States and its Western allies. Together, its members account for more than 40% of the world's population and almost a quarter of the global economy. The Chinese leader called the bloc a "leading group" in the Global South and a model of self-reliance among emerging and developing countries that should promote innovation-driven development. He said China would assume the BRICS chairmanship next year, and host the 19th BRICS summit, according to CCTV.

item.title: Trump tient l'Iran pour responsable de l'attaque contre un oléoduc saoudien
item.description: Le président américain Donald Trump a déclaré samedi que l'Iran était probablement responsable d'une attaque de drones contre l'Arabie saoudite qui a provoqué la fermeture de son oléoduc est-ouest, l'une des principales voies d'exportation de pétrole du royaume permettant de contourner le détroit d'Ormuz.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le président américain Donald Trump a déclaré samedi que l'Iran était probablement responsable d'une attaque de drones contre l'Arabie saoudite qui a provoqué la fermeture de son oléoduc est-ouest, l'une des principales voies d'exportation de pétrole du royaume permettant de contourner le détroit d'Ormuz. "Je pense que c'est eux, c'est probablement eux", a-t-il dit à la presse à Dublin à propos de cette attaque menée à partir du territoire irakien. Le président américain a précisé qu'il s'était entretenu avec le prince héritier saoudien Mohammed ben Salmane, après avoir répété que les États-Unis "contrôlent le détroit d'Ormuz". Donald Trump a par ailleurs affirmé que les Houthis, alliés de l'Iran qui pourraient bientôt être en mesure de fermer le [USN:L8N4530M9 TEXT:"détroit de Bab el-Mandeb"], porte d'entrée de la mer Rouge, avaient contacté son administration pour lui faire savoir qu'ils ne souhaitaient pas que les États-Unis s'impliquent directement dans le conflit au Yémen. "Ils préfèreraient de loin que nous ne nous en mêlions pas, et ils laissent passer la plupart des navires. Il n'y a qu'un seul pays avec lequel ils ne s'entendent pas très bien (l'Arabie saoudite, NDLR), et nous allons régler ce problème", a-t-il déclaré.

item.title: Silver lining: Olyslagers' runner-up finish brings unexpected reward
item.description: Australian high jumper Nicola Olyslagers thought she had endured one of the more frustrating nights of her glittering career on Friday but it turned out to be the most lucrative.
item.dc:creator: Lori Ewing
item.content:encoded: Australian high jumper Nicola Olyslagers thought she had endured one of the more frustrating nights of her glittering career on Friday but it turned out to be the most lucrative. The world champion posted 1.95 metres in the women's high jump at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship, struggling with her approach, while Ukraine's Olympic champion Yaroslava Mahuchikh cleared 1.99m to claim the title. Yet while Olyslagers missed out on becoming athletics' first "Ultimate" high jump champion on a chilly evening, the 29-year-old's second-place finish still delivered a career-best payday. When reporters informed her runners-up would pocket $75,000, the Australian's disappointment quickly gave way to delight. "What? Really? I genuinely thought it was just first prize got the 150k and second was like 10,000," Olyslagers told reporters. "You are the bearer of good news. That's fantastic." The cheque is worth $5,000 more than she earned for winning the world title last year. The surprise windfall was exactly the sort of moment World Athletics hoped to create when it launched the Ultimate Championship, a compact, television-friendly event with a record $10 million prize fund, the richest purse ever in track & field. Winners collect $150,000, while the runners-up get $75,000 and third-place finishers pocket $40,000, with athletes paid throughout the placings, a big shift for a sport that has long lagged behind others like tennis and golf in financial rewards. The sums have become a talking point around Budapest. Britain's Success Eduan earned $6,000 for helping her team finish third in the mixed 4x100 relay and already knows where some of the money could go -- to pay off her student loans. "Absolutely (the cash prize helps)," she said. But it wasn't really about the prize fund. It was more about the team. This event has been really, really good." The trainee midwife still has four babies to deliver next week before completing her degree at Salford University. British 1,500m runner Georgia Hunter Bell acknowledged the stakes had added an extra layer of excitement to the weekend. "You know $150,000, that means this is one you want to win so that's an added element," said Hunter Bell, who will race in the women's 1,500m final on Saturday. "I think mine and my husband's future home is going to look a bit different depending on how it goes here, which is really fun." Even with the championship's record-breaking purse, athletics still has some catching up to do compared with the biggest money-spinning sports. Players who lost in the first round of the U.S. Open singles draw, for instance, earned $140,000. Still, for athletes more accustomed to chasing titles than riches, World Athletics' new event has provided a rare chance to dream about both. For Olyslagers, who arrived in the mixed zone believing she had missed out on a golden opportunity, the night's biggest leap may have come after the competition ended, when she discovered just how much the silver was worth.

item.title: Trump says Iran probably responsible for attack on Saudi pipeline
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Iran was probably responsible for an aerial attack on Saudi Arabia that shut down its East-West pipeline, one of the kingdom's main routes for exporting crude while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Iran was probably responsible for an [USN:L6N453173 TEXT:"aerial attack"] on Saudi Arabia that shut down its East-West pipeline, one of the kingdom's main routes for exporting crude while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. "I think they are, probably they are," Trump told reporters in Dublin when asked if Iran was responsible for the attack on the vital oil conduit. The U.S. president also said that he had spoken with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom he described as a "good friend." Trump added that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis had called his admnistration and indicated they did not want the United States to become directly involved in the conflict. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through. There's just one country that they're not too happy with, and we'll get that straightened out," Trump added.

item.title: Bezzecchi smashes San Marino lap record to take pole ahead of Marquez
item.description: Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi fired a warning to his MotoGP championship rivals by breaking the all-time lap record at his home track of Misano on Saturday to take pole position for the San Marino Grand Prix ahead of Ducati's Marc Marquez.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi fired a warning to his MotoGP championship rivals by breaking the all-time lap record at his home track of Misano on Saturday to take pole position for the San Marino Grand Prix ahead of Ducati's Marc Marquez. Bezzecchi became the first rider to break the one minute and 30 seconds barrier, clocking 1:29.982 to give Aprilia pole on the team's home turf. "It was a good lap, I'm happy because the qualifying wasn't easy. I met a lot of yellow flags and it was difficult to find the concentration," Bezzecchi said. "In the first stint I stayed on the track one lap more just to have a lap time and fortunately it was my best one because in the second stint I couldn't have a clean lap." The Italian complained by raising his hand when LCR Honda's Johann Zarco impeded him and the stewards said they were investigating the incident. Bezzecchi will be joined by Marquez and Gresini Racing's Fermin Aldeguer on the front row. Marquez attempted to better his time twice late in the session but pulled out of both flying laps as he tried to ride over the limits on the turns. "Last year my pace was a bit better, but this year it looks like Marco is super fast, extremely fast in the fast corners," Marquez said. "Let's see if we can fight, but the target was the front row. When I stopped in the box, I saw the 1:29 (from Bezzecchi). I said, 'OK, ciao pole position, I will not arrive there because I knew where was my limits.' "I override, I tried to push my 100%. It was enough to achieve the target, not enough to be in pole position." VR46 Racing's Fabio Di Giannantonio went fourth fastest while championship leader Jorge Martin was only fifth fastest and has Honda's Luca Marini alongside him on the second row. Martin leads the championship with 256 points while Marquez is second (237 points) and Bezzecchi third (232 points). KTM's Pedro Acosta, VR46 Racing's Franco Morbidelli and Gresini Racing's Alex Marquez -- who crashed twice in the qualifying session -- will start on the third row. Francesco Bagnaia, who held the previous lap record at Misano, continued to struggle aboard his Ducati -- as he has all season -- and will start 14th on the grid after failing to advance from Q1 to Q2.

item.title: Canadian boycott of US products pushes grocers to adapt, explore new supply sources
item.description: A growing consumer push to buy Canadian and boycott U.S. products is reshaping supermarket shelves in Canada, forcing grocers to improve country-of-origin labeling and secure new sources of supply.
item.dc:creator: Nivedita Balu
item.content:encoded: A growing consumer push to buy Canadian and boycott U.S. products is reshaping supermarket shelves in Canada, forcing grocers to improve country-of-origin labeling and secure new sources of supply. In Ontario, the president of independent grocer Vince's Market, Giancarlo Trimarchi, turned to Facebook to show customers that most produce on his stores' shelves is Canadian after receiving angry emails and comments about the grocer stocking U.S. produce. A bitter trade war between the U.S. and Canada has made consumers more conscious of where their dollars go. "Buy Canadian" movements started [USN:L3N3QA1MV TEXT:"early last year"] after U.S. President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods and have intensified in recent weeks after trade talks [USN:L1N44J034 TEXT:"broke down"] and Trump signed an executive order renaming as Lake America. "It is a lot more aggressive this time around than last year," Trimarchi said in an interview. His four stores, spread across the Greater Toronto Area, now have about 90% Canadian produce. He is now sourcing strawberries from Quebec instead of the U.S. and has cut his advertising budget as the changes have pressured operating costs, he said. "We were always put in a position where you had to balance quality versus price. Now it's quality versus price versus country of origin," Trimarchi said. Loblaw Cos (L.TO) , the country's largest food retailer, brought back large signs featuring a maple leaf in its produce and fresh food sections in August after a brief hiatus to flag the products' Canadian origins. Loblaw also reintroduced a "T" tag to inform customers which products are affected by tariffs and make Canadian products easier to identify. Metro, the country's third-largest grocer, said it would continue to prioritize local Canadian products in the current context. "There has been a permanent change in the Canadian psyche," said Gary Sands, senior vice president of public policy and advocacy for the Canadian Federation of Independent Grocers. Canada is the world's fifth-largest importer of fresh vegetables by value. The U.S. is still the biggest supplier of fresh produce, accounting for more than half of the imports, followed by Mexico. However, the share of Canada's vegetable imports from the U.S. fell to 62.6% in July, the latest government data showed, from 69% in the same month of 2023, before Trump was elected. More than half of the country's fruit imports came from the U.S. as of July. Trade talks broke down on August 21, spurring a new round of tariffs and counter tariffs. John Ambard, 27, a software engineer who lives in downtown Toronto, said he has tried to avoid buying American products when possible, preferring to support Canadian brands and businesses. He said he checks product labels and researches companies online to identify Canadian-made goods. "I think, honestly, if I can support Canadian products and Canadian institutions through these tough times, I think that's a way to help in my small way," he said. “I'm a little bit mad with America right now with how things are going. The attitude has just not been that of a friend.” NEW SUPPLY CHAINS Canada's harsh winters present a challenge for fresh produce, and grocers typically rely on greenhouses, stocked root vegetables or imports, which are usually more cost-effective. But the change in sentiment toward the U.S. could push grocers to explore more local suppliers, experts say, while Canada invests in building a more self-reliant food system. The Canadian government is investing about C$3 billion over [USN:L6N42J17C TEXT:"10 years"] to build greenhouses to increase production during the harsh winter months. It is also trying to lower food inflation - among the highest in the Group of Seven developed nations - by increasing the domestic food supply. Gordon Dean, the owner of Mike Dean Local Grocer, which operates stores in rural Ontario and Quebec, said his stores are now selling more produce from countries like Spain, Brazil and Honduras than they previously did. "There's nobody running back to the U.S. supply chain because once the new supply chains are established, they're far more diversified. We're in a safer position," he said. However, Dean said restrictions and differing regulations between provinces made it harder to move food products across Canada, leaving many grocers reliant on suppliers south of the border. "Nationalism is now trumping economics to a degree that might switch if the relationship improves," said Mike von Massow, professor of Food Agriculture and Resource Economics at the University of Guelph. He said the Canada-U.S. relationship may never fully return to where it was, but a future easing of tensions, particularly under a new U.S. administration, could prompt a shift back to American products because they are often cheaper than other alternatives.

item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: Wall Street’s new gods
item.description: Firms like Apollo Global Management have elbowed their way into territory previously patrolled by big banks. This week’s update finds fresh insights in a new book about the $1 trln asset manager. Plus: why the foldable iPhone is like bifocal glasses, and the legacy of 9/11.
item.dc:creator: Peter Thal Larsen
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! The oil price is above $100 again, and the yield on 10-year U.S. government bonds is [USN:L6N4520W1 TEXT:"nearing 5%"]. When and where do higher inflation and interest rates begin to bite? Email me with your thoughts. If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend. OPENING LINE “Mark Carney is adding his name to the many special interests meddling in U.S. elections.” Read more: [USN:L6N4510XP TEXT:"Canada’s trade arsenal packs US political punch"]. FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK A year after their $54 billion mining merger, Anglo American (AAL.L) and Teck Resources (TECKb.TO) are still waiting for Chinese approval. ([USN:L6N4500SP TEXT:"Megadeals are getting harder"]) Loan growth in China fell to a record low of 5.1% in July. ([USN:L4N44Z04Q TEXT:"A bank recap won’t help"]) The four largest U.S. airlines control 80% of their domestic market; Europe’s top six groups have only 70%. ([USN:L6N44Z0JV TEXT:"Mergers are inevitable"]) Smart-ring maker Oura boasts a 46% gross margin. ([USN:L6N4500TJ TEXT:"Still a peddler of gadgets"]) Hong Kong has been the world’s least affordable housing market for 16 consecutive years. ([USN:L4N451034 TEXT:"Legacy of failed reforms"]) APOLLO’S GIANT LEAP The term “Wall Street” still tends to evoke images of investment bankers in expensive suits and traders yelling into phones. That snapshot is seriously out of date, though. In recent years a new batch of upstart institutions have elbowed their way into the territory previously patrolled by big banks. A new book sheds fresh light on one of them: Apollo Global Management (APO.N) . The outlines of Apollo’s story are well known. Founded by former executives of Drexel Burnham Lambert, the junk bond pioneer which collapsed in 1990, it dabbled in private equity and distressed debt before expanding into other forms of lending. Its growth has been largely fueled by a captive insurance unit, Athene, which steers cash from annuities and other products into Apollo’s private bonds and loans. Under Marc Rowan, who replaced Leon Black as CEO in 2021, assets under management have swelled to more than $1 trillion. William D. Cohan’s “ Money To Burn: The Unvarnished Truth about Leon Black, Apollo, and the Rise of a New Wall Street ” sheds fresh light on the human drama behind Apollo’s ascent, from the firm’s scrappy origins to Black’s relationship with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. It’s arguably the first deeply reported history of one of Wall Street’s new shadow banks. (I talked to Bill about his book on The Big View this week. Check out our conversation on YouTube or read the transcript here .) Three observations stand out. The first is how the Drexel wreck shaped Apollo, in part by opening up lucrative investments. The firm’s early financial successes included buying a portfolio of distressed debt from Executive Life, a failed insurance company which had bought many of Drexel’s junk bonds. Apollo paid roughly $3 billion for the securities – about half their face value – pocketing a big profit when values recovered. In doing so, Black somehow steered the firm around a regulatory scandal involving Executive Life which sucked in the French bank Credit Lyonnais. The second takeaway is how Rowan’s deep knowledge of the insurance industry laid the foundations for the creation of Athene, which has provided much of the financial fuel for Apollo’s push into private credit. Though that model has been widely imitated by others, Rowan’s vision pioneered it. The jury is still out on the durability of Apollo’s business model, though. Rowan makes a compelling case that matching long-term insurance liabilities with borrowers through private funds is less risky than intermediating the same loans through leveraged banks. Envious bankers, meanwhile, argue Apollo is mimicking Michael Milken, Drexel’s junk bond mastermind, by funnelling risky loans to unsophisticated investors. It will probably take an economic downturn – and perhaps another book – to settle that debate. CHART OF THE WEEK Unless you have been living in a cave for the past week you have probably heard about Apple’s (AAPL.O) new foldable iPhone. Rivals like Samsung have offered similar products for some time. But Rob Cyran thinks he knows who might want bigger screens: ageing users with deteriorating eyesight. Buying Apple’s new gadget is therefore the modern equivalent of [USN:L6N45012A TEXT:"wearing bifocal glasses"]. Ouch. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS Nvidia (NVDA.O) is the undisputed champion of artificial intelligence chips. Now the $5 trillion company is using its vast financial resources to support customers and stimulate enduring demand for its products. Karen Kwok joined Aimee Donnellan and Jonathan Guilford in the Viewsroom this week to debate whether Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s financial alchemy can fend off competitors and defend the company’s enviable margins. Over on The Big View , I talked to William D. Cohan about his new book on Apollo Global Management. PARTING SHOT Twenty-five years ago I was working as a journalist in New York when two hijacked planes flew into the World Trade Center. The anniversary of the tragedy and its aftermath always brings back powerful memories of the destruction I observed in downtown Manhattan, the eerie silence as the city ground to a halt, and the many acts of kindness and humanity I experienced from ordinary New Yorkers. Those sentiments faded as the United States embarked on two epically destructive and expensive wars. A quarter of a century on, [USN:L6N44H12P TEXT:"Gabriel Rubin assesses"] the long-term effects of the 9/11 attacks on the country’s finances – and on its defence industry. Want to receive The Week in Breakingviews in your inbox every Saturday? Sign up for the newsletter here . Follow Peter Thal Larsen on Bluesky and LinkedIn .

item.title: Hong Kong like a local
item.dc:creator: Farah Master
item.content:encoded: REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans Hong Kong — which means “fragrant harbour” in Chinese — is known for its glistening financial centre and densely packed skyline. But beneath this glimmering facade lies another Hong Kong: one of sprawling, green country parks, world-class hiking, and over 260 islands that form a paradise for open-water swimming. I was born and raised here, and after stints for Reuters in London, Beijing and Shanghai, returned here in 2013 to cover breaking news. I grew up hiking Hong Kong’s nature trails, taking my golden retriever swimming at local beaches and tucking into bamboo baskets of char siu bao (barbecued pork bun) and har gao (shrimp dumplings). While the city’s political fabric has shifted dramatically following 2019 pro-democracy protests , the passage of a 2020 national security law and the COVID-19 pandemic, Hong Kong is beginning to regain its mojo, drawing back international visitors and expatriates alike. Here’s how to explore Hong Kong like a local: The way around: Hong Kong boasts one of the world’s cleanest and most efficient public transportation networks. It begins with the Airport Express train , which whisks you from the international airport straight into the Central business district in just 24 minutes, with fares costing up to HK$130 ($16.50). Tourists take selfies along the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu A woman holding incense walks through Man Mo Temple. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu People walk along a street in Hong Kong's Soho district, decorated with temporary neon lights and market stalls for a film production. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu A Peak Tram car ascends towards Victoria Peak with the Hong Kong skyline in the background. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu Tourists walk past stalls selling Hong Kong-themed souvenirs at the Ladies' Market in Hong Kong's Mong Kok district. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu Tourists walk past stalls at the Ladies' Market in Hong Kong's Mong Kok district. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu Tourists board a sightseeing boat on Victoria Harbour. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu Tourists watch the sunset over Victoria Harbour. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu People walk along a street in Hong Kong's Soho district, decorated with temporary neon lights and market stalls for a film production. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu Tourists ride a Star Ferry with Hong Kong's Central financial district in the background, China, July 24, 2026. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu A tram passes the Court of Final Appeal in Hong Kong's Central district. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu A dog walks past people on Repulse Bay Beach. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu Tourists take pictures of Hong Kong's skyline from Victoria Peak. REUTERS/Tyrone Siu The underground rail network, the Mass Transit Railway (MTR) , is so famously punctual that if a train pauses for even 30 seconds longer than scheduled, an automated announcement immediately apologises and asks passengers for their patience. Air-conditioned double-decker buses traverse the entire territory, while the tram — known locally as the “ding ding” — is a charming, slow-paced way to take in the sounds, smells and sights of Hong Kong Island. Visitors can pay for both using an Octopus card (buy it at the airport, MTR customer service centres or convenience stores like 7-Eleven) or by using contactless payment. For a more scenic journey, board the historic Star Ferry , connecting Hong Kong Island to the bustling Kowloon peninsula, or hop on a ferry out to the tranquil outlying islands of Lantau or Lamma. Into nature: For a classic introduction to Hong Kong’s peaks, take a stroll up the Morning Trail from Hatton Road to Victoria Peak, where you can find incredible views of Victoria Harbour. From there, you could continue up to Victoria Peak Garden , a quiet Victorian-style park featuring open lawns and panoramic views. To head back down to Central, ride the historic Peak Tram , one of the world’s oldest funicular railways, which climbs gradients of up to 25.7 degrees. Repulse Bay , a 20-minute bus ride from Central, is a favourite year-round beach spot. After swimming, grab a coffee or tea at Neighbourhood , just across from the beach, or a bite at one of the many beachside cafes. For a scenic day hike, try the Dragon’s Back , an 8km (5-mile) trail that snakes along the ridge of Shek O Peak and descends to the white sands of Big Wave Bay, a popular surf spot adjacent to Shek O village and its laid-back eateries. If time permits, a trip to Tai Long Wan bay on the Sai Kung peninsula is also a must. With its turquoise waters and pristine beaches, you could easily mistake it for a Thai island. The easiest way to access it is via a speedboat from Sai Kung town, though be warned it can be a bit choppy on the water. Alternatively, you can hike in via several scenic routes from Sai Kung country park. Shopping spree: While many locals travel across the border to Shenzhen for shopping, Hong Kong remains a retail hub. For electronics, head to the Wan Chai Computer Centre . For sneakers and streetwear, try Fa Yuen Street (known as Sneakers Street) in Mong Kok. If you're looking for vibrant neighbourhood culture, explore Sham Shui Po’s independent shops and quirky cafes. Or beat the subtropical heat in air-conditioned malls like Pacific Place, IFC and Times Square. Get artsy: Hong Kong has rapidly expanded its arts offerings over the years, most notably with the contemporary art M+ Museum and the Hong Kong Palace Museum , which offers Chinese historical artwork as well as special exhibitions including ancient Egyptian civilisations in West Kowloon. The underground rail network, the Mass Transit Railway (MTR), is so famously punctual that if a train pauses for even 30 seconds longer than scheduled, an automated announcement immediately apologises and asks passengers for their patience. On Hong Kong island, Tai Kwun is a meticulously restored colonial-era police station turned heritage and arts centre. Nearby, the historic Fringe Club hosts indie art exhibitions and live music. For a unique architectural experience, visit the Asia Society in Admiralty, housed within former 19th-century British military buildings. Good eats: From Dai pai dongs (open-air food stalls) to world-class fine dining, Hong Kong is a culinary powerhouse. While the Chinese food is stellar, the city’s international community ensures access to excellent Thai, Japanese, Korean, Indian and Lebanese cuisine as well. For dim sum, Tim Ho Wan remains a budget-friendly favourite, while Lin Heung Tea House offers a nostalgic experience where servers wheel traditional metal trolleys piled high with bamboo steamer baskets. For a more upscale experience, head to Madam Fu at Tai Kwun for contemporary Cantonese cuisine. I recommend trying the smoked bean curd roll with shiitake mushroom and carrot and the wagyu beef mapo tofu. If you are craving Southeast Asian flavours, Samsen serves delicious flat beef or vegetable rice noodles, while Arirang does a great traditional Korean barbecue. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population: 7.5 million people Price of a coffee: HK$35 ($5) for a macchiato at Frenchies on Hollywood Road or HK$30 ($3.80) for a coffee at local chain Fineprint. Price of an ice cream: HK$58 ($7.40) for a scoop at Snack Baby Gelato , which has unique local flavours including Szechuan chilli mango and five-spice mandarin. Great place to see a sunset: Tsim Sha Tsui promenade offers great views of the Hong Kong skyline at night. Largest university: University of Hong Kong, 45,000 students

item.title: Jay Rayner on the responsibility of restaurant criticism
item.description: The veteran British food critic discusses his new book, how the pandemic changed his approach to negative reviews, and the places he won’t cover.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Serhan
item.content:encoded: British food critic Jay Rayner poses for a photograph at his home in London, Britain, August 19, 2026. REUTERS/Hannah McKay Jay Rayner, by his own admission, doesn’t get invited to too many dinner parties. The veteran British restaurant critic — whose more than a quarter-century of reviews for The Observer and, more recently, the Financial Times newspaper has earned him the nickname “Acid Rayner” — is known for his searing assessments of restaurants across the U.K. Among his most excoriating assessments was that he couldn’t describe one place as serving “the worst cooking in Britain,” if only because he hadn’t eaten in every restaurant in the land. But Rayner’s day job doesn’t mean he’ll turn his nose up atgood old-fashioned home cooking, which he pays homage to in his latest book “Nights Out in the Kitchen,” a part-cookbook, part-memoir featuring recipes for some of the best dishes from across his career, plus some original dishes. Speaking with Reuters from his home in South London ahead of his book tour , Rayner discusses the art of the review in the social media age, his philosophy for negative critiques, and the restaurants he won’t go near. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. British food critic Jay Rayner poses for a photograph at his home in London, Britain, August 19, 2026. REUTERS/Hannah McKay You’ve been a restaurant critic for more than a quarter century. How’d you get your start? I’m a print journalist. That is the thing I've always been. I chose my university because it had the biggest student newspaper, got elected editor, and I was then a general writer and reporter, advancing from very soft features into harder and harder news and long form and foreign reporting. I did it all apart from sport — and even then, I like to point out that I once did the all-amateur natural bodybuilding championship in Leeds. And then, (in 1999), I was taken out for lunch by the then editor of The Observer magazine, for whom I deputized on every column, and she said, "Our restaurant critic is moving on. Who should I get to do the job?" It was not my intention to put my hand up. But the moment she said that, I went, "Well, how about me?" What I discovered in food was that it covers everything: politics, economics, history, trade routes. When people look at the Arab Spring, they see it as a spontaneous uprising in response to a sudden desire for democracy. But if you drill down on it, it's actually about food price rises and the inability of authoritarian governments to keep their population in line when they could no longer give them bread at a reasonable price. And when you start to understand that, you think, this is a really interesting subject. And so it has continually become a part of my working life. Over 25 years, what's changed about what makes a good review? And what has stayed the same? Has anything changed about what makes a good review? I don't think it has, actually. I think the eternal verities (remain true), which is that you have to speak to the reader as though they're the only person reading, that you are telling them how much pleasure their money will give them. You're not writing for the tiny number of well-informed gastronomes — the "napkin sniffers," as I call them — but for the general reader and you need to understand it as a conversation with those readers. What I discovered in food was that it covers everything: politics, economics, history, trade routes Jay Rayner That said, a lot has changed about the way restaurants are covered, how much other coverage there is. Social media has played a big part in that. With the rise of content creation, these days most anyone can be a critic. Do you see that as a challenge? It is only a challenge if it's better than me. I cannot just claim, "Look, I'm the guy from the big newspaper and therefore I have a right to be read." Every writer has to make an argument for their writing to be read every single time they write. Nobody has to read a single thing you write — not even your mother. There's a lot of stuff out there, and some of it's good and some of it's bad. Generally, I like to think that the audience will spot the rubbish. There are certain influencer review sites where I think, "Oh God, this is awful,” but it's got 2.5 million followers, so they must like something about it. Your new book reads as part-cookbook, part memoir. What are you hoping readers take from it, apart from some delicious home cooking recipes? This is the sequel to "Nights Out at Home," which happened because I was heading towards 25 years (as a restaurant critic), and what I realized was I genuinely have this habit of, if I come across a good idea in a restaurant, I'll take it home and reverse engineer that idea. I thought, actually, that's a brilliant way (of) telling the stories of these restaurants you love. It's a very broad selection of dishes, plus, with this one, 20 of the (recipes) are officially mine. They're things that I cook or have always cooked. In one chapter, you reflect on some of the more brutal reviews you’ve given. You mean the chapter headed, "Am I a total bastard?" British food critic Jay Rayner poses for a photograph with his new book Nights Out in the Kitchen, at his home in London, Britain, August 19, 2026. REUTERS/Hannah McKay That's the one. It got me wondering: How do you approach writing a negative review? Have you ever returned to a restaurant that received one to see if it improved? I've done it only once. It was a place where they’d advertised themselves as being a great Italian new wave restaurant. I went there and concluded it was just a bar, and they weren't really interested in the food. That was the review. The owner wrote to me and said, "You're absolutely right, but we are now," and I went back and it was. The interesting thing, at least to me, is I wouldn't have bothered with that first review now. If I'd gone there and had that experience, I would have paid the bill and never written about it. So the major difference now, and I think it's a lot to do with COVID and coming out of (the pandemic), is if you're going to write a negative review, you better have a bloody good reason for it. And the motto is: punch up, not down. The small mom-and-pop place that's not doing very well or isn't making it, let them fail by themselves. But if you come across somewhere like (the high-end London restaurant) Jul's — this mad, insane place apparently born out of some landmark restaurant in Ibiza where they were doing terrible things to the food at excruciating prices, I didn't have any concerns about writing what I felt . And the point I said in the review was: money might end up being spent here that should be spent elsewhere. Now that's a bit brutal, but it's true. You write about the #MeToo reckoning in kitchens. Has that changed how you review a restaurant — what you're looking for, what you're weighing? It is complicated because, generally, you do not know what's going on in a restaurant. It's like a family: You can't necessarily tell it's dysfunctional if you just go over for tea. Maybe you can sense it. There are certain chefs I will not review because I think they're monstrous individuals. If you are a nightmarish figure, I'm not going near you. That all sounds very grand and moral. The problem is you can't always tell. What kinds of cuisines do you think are still unrepresented or underrepresented in the places you review? The entirety of Africa. We obviously have very developed African communities in the U.K., but the restaurants representing the food of Africa tend to be mediated in some way. Sichuan food (in London) will bear similarities to what you find in Chengdu, whereas a Nigerian restaurant that ends up in Soho is unlikely to be what you'll find in the back streets of Lagos. I'm not sure why that is. Now for some rapid-fire questions. What’s your death-row meal? You can find it in my book, "My Last Supper: One Meal, a Lifetime in the Making." It would involve garlicky snails, a bacon sandwich properly made on white bread, and a Mont Blanc to finish. Who would you invite to your dream dinner party? Dorothy Parker, but only until the end of the starters, because after that she'll be drunk and just a bit annoying. Peter Ustinov, who was a great British actor, wit, and raconteur. Ella Fitzgerald, because I have a sideline as a jazz pianist and I'd love to play alongside her. Gene Harris, who is a fantastic, bluesy jazz pianist. And if I'm allowed fictional, Baloo the Bear from "The Jungle Book." Another is Dita Von Teese. After Dorothy Parker has had to retire, Dita can take over. What’s your favorite restaurant of late? My most recent top experience is a place called IGNI . It is a live-fire tasting menu restaurant (in London) by a chef called Theo Clench. I normally have no time or patience for the whole tasting menu thing — I find it tiresome and performative, and all the performance doesn't match up to the joy of the food. But this one really, really did. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Trump arrives in Ireland to meet leaders before attending golf tournament
item.description: DUBLIN: US President Donald Trump arrived in Dublin on Saturday (Sep 12), where he will meet Ireland's leaders before attending a golf tournament at one of his resorts, a detour from his
item.dc:creator: CNA

DUBLIN: US President Donald Trump arrived in Dublin on Saturday (Sep 12), where he will meet Ireland's leaders before attending a golf tournament at one of his resorts, a detour from his recent focus on the Iran war and his party's effort to maintain power in November's midterm elections.  The meetings with Ireland's president and prime minister are not part of an official state visit. But coming after this week's Republican convention and the 25th anniversary of the Sep 11 attacks , the talks could include politically sensitive topics such as economic issues and Irish leaders' concerns over the Iran war.  Trump is making his 48-hour foreign trip as his Republican Party campaigns to keep its majorities in both chambers of the US Congress. The Iran conflict has heightened economic concerns among American voters by raising gas prices nationwide. He was greeted by Ireland's deputy prime minister and foreign minister on the tarmac at Dublin Airport.

Anti-war and anti- Trump protests are planned in Dublin and in western Ireland near the Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg.  Ireland is one of the European Union's most pro-Palestinian countries and passed a law in July curbing goods trade with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. US lawmakers and the American ambassador to Ireland criticised the law.

U.S. President Donald Trump participates in an arrival ceremony at Aras an Uachtarain in Dublin, Ireland, on Sep 12, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Kylie Cooper)

US, IRELAND TIES Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin has so far avoided political flaps with the US. "The relationship between Ireland and the United States is very important economically," Martin told reporters when asked about Trump 's weekend trip. "It's very, very significant both ways." US-owned companies employ about 10 per cent of workers in Ireland after successive governments prioritised their jobs and corporate tax revenue over decades, handing Ireland the healthiest public finances in Europe in recent years.  In Dublin on Saturday, Trump will meet Irish President Catherine Connolly, who was elected head of state last year. When Trump last visited as president in 2019, Connolly, an outspoken politician with far-left views on foreign policy, protested outside Shannon Airport in western Ireland. Some supporters have urged her to speak up against US military actions around the world and defend Ireland's neutrality. Including Trump , eight sitting US presidents have visited Ireland, starting with John F Kennedy in 1963. But this trip has some hallmarks of Trump 's typical weekends, which often revolve around golf outings at his company's properties.   The Trump Organization took control in 2014 of the Doonbeg course, which is hosting the Irish Open golf tournament this weekend. Trump is expected to help present the trophy on Sunday to the tournament champion.
